title: The Meaning of October 12
author: Felipe Ávila
content:
_This article by[Felipe
Ávila](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Felipe%20%C3%81vila) originally
appeared in the [October 12, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/12/opinion/significado-
del-12-de-octubre), Mexico’s premier left wing daily newspaper._

On October 12, 1492, the Genoese navigator Christopher Columbus, at the head
of a naval expedition of three caravels sent by the monarchs of Castile and
Aragon, Ferdinand and Isabella, reached the small island of Guanahaní, in the
Caribbean archipelago, which the expeditionaries named San Salvador. The
purpose of the voyage was to find an alternative commercial sea route to the
Indies, sailing west across the Atlantic Ocean. Columbus died believing he had
reached the Indies, an error that Amerigo Vespucci corrected years later,
demonstrating that the lands found were a continent, which the Europeans
called America.

The Europeans found human beings who surprised them by being naked, by the
darker tone of their skin, by a language they did not understand, and by a way
of life very different from the one Europeans of that era were accustomed to.

In accordance with what Columbus had agreed with the Catholic Monarchs in the
Capitulations of Santa Fe, he unilaterally took possession of the land they
had reached and, although Columbus did not say so in the testimony he sent to
the monarchs, he captured several native men by force and took them to Spain
to show them to the monarchs.

That first contact between the Europeans and the natives of what would become
America was a historic event that changed world history forever. **It was the
beginning of a relationship of colonial domination** , in which the Europeans
declared war, defeated, conquered and subjugated the native peoples,
dispossessed them of their lands, enslaved those who offered resistance,
exploited their labor, raped many of their women, prohibited and punished
their religious practices, imposed Christianity and a foreign government on
them, as well as laws and institutions to consolidate a system of colonial
domination over a large part of the American continent, a system that lasted
until the 1820s.

From that first contact, Columbus and the Europeans who accompanied him, and
who very soon returned in larger expeditions, felt superior to the Native
Americans. He informed Ferdinand and Isabella that they were people very
simple in arms and that with 50 Europeans they could subjugate them all and
force them to do whatever the Europeans wanted.

Less than a year later, Pope Alexander VI unilaterally granted full dominion
over the American lands, and over others that Castilian or Portuguese
navigators might discover, through the Bull Inter Caetera of May 4, 1493. In
it, the pope told the Catholic Monarchs that the Catholic faith and the
Christian religion must be spread everywhere to procure “the salvation of
souls and that the barbarous nations be humbled and brought to this faith… We
certainly know that you had proposed to seek and discover some mainlands and
remote and unknown islands, not discovered until now by others, in order to
bring their inhabitants to the worship of our Redeemer and the profession of
the Catholic faith.”

The pontiff referred to Columbus’s expedition, which found “certain very
remote islands and also mainlands that until now had not been discovered by
others, in which dwell many peoples who live peacefully and, as is asserted,
go naked and do not eat meat: and, as your aforementioned envoys can judge,
these peoples who inhabit the said islands and lands believe in one God the
Creator who is in heaven, and they consider them quite fit to embrace the
Catholic faith and to be imbued with good customs…”

On those islands they had found gold, perfumes and valuable things that
awakened the greed of the European invaders. For this reason, the pope
authorized continuing those expeditions with the incentive that those lands
–which were not empty, since they were populated by **millions of native
inhabitants who had lived on them for millennia** – would be the property of
the Castilian and Portuguese kingdoms, since he granted “with the fullness of
apostolic power: all the islands and mainlands, discovered and to be
discovered, found and to be found toward the west and south, drawing and
establishing a line from the Arctic Pole, that is, the North, to the Antarctic
Pole, that is, the South, whether they be on mainland or on islands discovered
and to be discovered toward India or toward any other part…”

On that basis began the process of exploration, territorial occupation, wars
of extermination, exploitation and subjugation of millions of human beings who
were considered inferior to European civilization, which they themselves
considered superior. **It was a brutal war of conquest and colonization
disguised as a just war** , a crusade to forcibly convert the natives to the
Christian religion.

The date that symbolized that process as its starting point was that October
12. The Europeans christened it the Discovery of America, ignoring that this
continent already existed, was densely populated, and that great civilizations
had developed on it. For centuries, the new masters of the territory
perpetuated the idea and meaning of that colonization by commemorating its
starting date, which they called “discovery.” It was not until 1992, on the
fifth centenary, that millions of Indigenous Americans mobilized and protested
against that celebration and gave it a new name and meaning, the one that has
gained general acceptance: **October 12 is the Day of Indigenous Resistance**
, which makes a 180-degree turn and underscores the process of resistance, of
survival, of struggle of the Indigenous peoples to maintain their culture,
their forms of organization, their history and their values, and that is the
meaning that must prevail.

    Felipe Ávila
